title: Port security, DHCP snooping and DAI

cards.heading: What port security does
cards.body: Port security limits which MAC addresses can send frames into a switch port and how many. It stops someone unplugging a desk PC and plugging in their own device, or flooding the MAC table.
cards.example:
interface fa0/3
 switchport mode access
 switchport port-security

cards.heading: Set the mode first
cards.body: Port security only works on static access (or trunk) ports. On a port left in the default dynamic mode, IOS rejects the command, so configure 'switchport mode access' first.
cards.example:
SW1(config-if)#switchport port-security
Command rejected: FastEthernet0/3 is a dynamic port.

cards.heading: Maximum and sticky addresses
cards.body: The default maximum is one MAC address. Sticky learning remembers the addresses it learns and writes them into the running configuration, so you don't have to type them in. Sticky addresses are only in the running configuration, so save it to keep them across a reload. With the defaults (maximum 1, violation shutdown) enabling port security plus sticky learning is enough to lock a port to the PC plugged in now.
cards.example:
switchport port-security maximum 2
 switchport port-security mac-address sticky

cards.heading: Violation modes
cards.body: When an extra MAC address shows up: protect drops its traffic silently; restrict drops it, logs it and counts the violation; shutdown (the default) puts the port into err-disabled. Recover an err-disabled port with shutdown then no shutdown. In 'show port-security interface', a Port Status of Secure-shutdown with a violation count means an unexpected MAC arrived and the port is err-disabled until it's bounced (or errdisable recovery brings it back).
cards.example:
protect   drop                    port stays up
restrict  drop + log + counter    port stays up
shutdown  err-disabled            port goes down (default)
cards.mnemonic:
Alphabetical order is also quiet to loud: Protect drops silently, Restrict drops and tells you (log and counter), Shutdown slams the door (err-disabled).
The default is the loudest: shutdown.

cards.heading: DHCP snooping
cards.body: DHCP snooping stops rogue DHCP servers. Every port is untrusted by default: the switch drops DHCP server messages (OFFER, ACK) that arrive on an untrusted port. Trust only the ports toward the real server. The switch also records each lease (MAC, IP, VLAN, port) in its binding table.
cards.example:
ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
!
interface g0/1
 ip dhcp snooping trust
!
show ip dhcp snooping binding

cards.heading: Dynamic ARP Inspection
cards.body: DAI stops ARP spoofing. On untrusted ports the switch checks each ARP message's sender MAC and IP against the DHCP snooping binding table and drops any that don't match. Trust the uplinks. DAI needs DHCP snooping (or static ARP ACLs) to have something to check against.
cards.example:
ip arp inspection vlan 10
!
interface g0/1
 ip arp inspection trust

cards.heading: Which feature stops which attack
cards.body: DHCP snooping stops rogue DHCP servers. Dynamic ARP Inspection stops ARP spoofing (man-in-the-middle). Port security stops MAC address table flooding by capping MACs per port. Root Guard (from the spanning tree lesson) stops an unauthorised switch taking over as root. The snooping binding table is learned from DHCP exchanges on untrusted ports, and DAI and IP Source Guard both use it to check traffic.
cards.example:
Rogue DHCP server ........ DHCP snooping
ARP spoofing ............. Dynamic ARP Inspection
MAC table flooding ....... Port security
Rogue root bridge ........ Root Guard
cards.mnemonic: Name what's being faked, and the feature that guards it says so. A fake DHCP server is stopped by DHCP snooping. Fake ARP replies are stopped by Dynamic ARP Inspection. Fake MACs flooding the table are stopped by Port security, which caps MACs per port. A fake root bridge is stopped by Root Guard.
